keyVerseText: And the LORD said furthermore unto him, Put now thine hand into thy bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom: and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous as snow.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb צָרַע (tsâraʻ) is a primitive root that primarily conveys the state of being afflicted with leprosy. Its core sense involves being 'stricken' or 'scourged,' specifically in the physical sense of a skin disease. This root meaning highlights not only the condition of leprosy but also the experience of being visibly marked or afflicted, which goes beyond the English gloss of 'leper' by emphasizing the passive suffering and divine judgment implied in the original Hebrew.
usageInScripture: Across its 20 occurrences, צָרַע consistently describes the condition of leprosy, either as a verb meaning 'to be leprous' or as a substantive meaning 'leper.' The top translations reflect this consistency, with frequent renderings such as 'and behold she was leprous,' 'being a leper,' and 'was leprous.' This uniformity in translation underscores the term's fixed association with the physical and ceremonial implications of leprosy in the biblical text, highlighting both the physical affliction and its social and religious consequences.
theologicalSignificance: The word צָרַע carries profound theological weight as it represents not only a physical disease but also a visible sign of separation and judgment under the Old Covenant. Its use in Scripture reminds believers of the holiness of God and the seriousness of sin, which can mar and isolate a person from the community. In the Christian faith, this word points forward to the ultimate healing and restoration found in Christ, who bore our afflictions and cleansed us from spiritual uncleanness. Understanding צָרַע deepens appreciation for Christ’s work in overcoming the curse of sin and restoring fellowship with God.
keyVerseReflection: Exodus 4:6 states, 'And the LORD said furthermore unto him, Put now thine hand into thy bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom: and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous as snow.' Here, the word צָרַע vividly illustrates a miraculous sign of God's power, transforming Moses' hand to appear leprous. This use highlights the word's meaning as a visible, unmistakable mark of affliction, serving as a divine demonstration that commands attention and signals God's authority. It reminds us that God can both afflict and heal, using even the sign of leprosy to accomplish His purposes.
